0.0.n: This is his family name, placed before his given name in Japanese.

0.1.n: This is his given name, following his family name.

0.2.n: A polite sentence ending used here to introduce himself.

1.0.n: Introduces an imagined situation, with slightly more emphasis than もし.

1.1.n: Combines with 選手 to name the sport the player competes in.

1.2.n: Refers to a sports competitor; 野球選手 is the complete job description.

1.3.n: A conversational contraction of では; with なかったら, it forms the negative condition.

1.4.n: This is the stem of ない used before たら in the negative condition.

1.5.n: Completes なかったら, making the negative condition; its past-looking form does not necessarily describe past time.

1.7.n: Asks which alternative occupation he would have chosen.

1.8.n: Marks the resulting role with なる, the verb for becoming.

1.9.n: Short for なっていました, the polite past form of なっている; the imagined condition gives it a hypothetical reading.

1.10.n: Ends the sentence as a polite question.

2.0.n: An interjection showing he is thinking about his answer.

2.2.n: In そうだね, it helps him acknowledge the question while considering his answer.

2.3.n: The plain counterpart of です, used in the casual response そうだね.

2.4.n: Softens そうだ and gives the response a thoughtful, conversational feel.

2.6.n: Combines with 選手 to identify the sport.

2.7.n: Together with ラグビー, this names his possible alternative career.

2.8.n: Works with the following な to make かな, expressing a tentative answer.

2.9.n: Completes かな, giving the answer a reflective rather than certain tone.

3.0.n: A casual affirmative response, less formal than はい.

3.2.n: Japanese often leaves out possessives when the family relationship is clear.

3.3.n: Identifies his father as the person who played rugby.

3.4.n: The activity performed with やる; the object particle を is omitted in casual speech.

3.5.n: Short for やっていて; it describes an ongoing activity and connects to what follows.

4.0.n: Links his own rugby experience to the fact that his father played.

4.2.n: Describes his age in 小さい頃, rather than simply his physical size.

4.3.n: A noun for a period of time; 小さい頃 refers to his early childhood.

4.4.n: Marks early childhood as the starting point.

4.6.n: Names the youngest standard preschool class, generally for children aged three to four.

4.7.n: Marks the more specific starting point: his first preschool year.

4.8.n: Emphasizes that he continued playing over an extended period.

4.9.n: The activity he played; casual speech leaves out the object particle を here.

4.10.n: Short for やっていて; this connecting form describes his continuing childhood activity.

5.0.n: A shortened まあ, used as a casual filler before his assessment.

5.2.n: Adds a fairly strong degree to his description of his skill.

5.3.n: The past form of うまい, referring here to skill at rugby.

5.4.n: Short for の; with だ, it presents his skill as background information.

5.5.n: Combines with ん to give the statement an explanatory tone.

5.6.n: Trails off softly, leaving a contrast implied rather than stating it directly.

6.0.n: Signals that he is imagining an alternative to his actual baseball career.

6.1.n: Stands for choosing baseball as his sport or career.

6.2.n: Short for では; combines with なかったら to set up a negative condition.

6.3.n: The stem of ない before たら, contributing the negative part of the condition.

6.4.n: Completes なかったら, making an imagined condition rather than simply reporting the past.

6.6.n: Combines with でも to emphasize continuation into the present.

6.7.n: In 今でも, it indicates that the activity would still be continuing now.

6.8.n: The activity he imagines continuing; the object particle を is omitted.

6.9.n: The て-form of やる; with the following た, it forms casual やってた, shortened from やっていた.

6.10.n: This splits into た + かな + って: a hypothetical past ending, uncertainty, and a thought quotation; not たかなる.

6.11.n: The polite form of 思う; って introduces the thought he is expressing.

0.tip: Japanese introductions often omit I and put the family name before the given name.

1.lit: If not a baseball player, what would you have become?
1.tip: じゃなかったら sets up an imagined alternative: if you were not something.

2.lit: Ah, so it is, you know. A rugby player, perhaps.
2.tip: Ending with かな makes his answer sound tentative and thoughtful.

3.lit: Yeah, my father played rugby, and...
3.tip: やってて is short for やっていて and connects this background detail to the next part.

4.lit: So, from when little, from first-year preschool, all along playing rugby, and...
4.tip: The understood subject shifts from his father to himself without an explicit I.

5.lit: Well, pretty good was, you see, though.
5.tip: Sentence-final けど can soften a statement and trail off without an explicit contrasting clause.

6.lit: If not baseball, even now rugby would have been playing, perhaps, I think.
6.tip: Despite its past-looking form, やってた refers to imagined ongoing play now because of the condition and 今でも.
